newsitem.title: UK: BAe, Rolls gain on hopes for end to foreign limit.
newsitem.headline: BAe, Rolls gain on hopes for end to foreign limit.

text.p: Shares in aerospace groups British Aerospace Plc and Rolls Royce Plc were in demand on Monday amid speculation that the British government might relax limits on foreign ownership of their shares.

Press reports said the two companies believed that the limits, designed to prevent control of strategically important industries falling into overseas hands, were outmoded and were lobbying the government for change.
BAe spokesman Mike Peters told Reuters on Sunday that it believed it would be advantageous if the foreign ownership limits no longer applied.
"Both Rolls Royce and British Aerospace have had discussions with the government about the situation," Peters told Reuters.
A report in the Sunday Times said the two companies believed the limit was an obstacle to shareholder value and could restrict their scope for strategic expansion.

It said overseas investors held about 26 percent of both companies and that scrapping the limit could release pent-up overseas demand. Foreign shareholders are currently restricted to holding 29.5 percent of the two companies.

British Aerospace shares reached a record 12.89 pounds in early trading though they later drifted back, with the stock having difficulty building on its recent sharp gains, partly because of cautious comment on the stock in the Financial Times.

The FT's influential Lex column said the stock looked fully valued and that the euphoria linked to Boeing Co's recent bid for McDonnell Douglas Corp was overdone since "there is no European Boeing about to snap it up".
By 1100 GMT BAe shares were down 9.5 pence at 12.70 pounds.
Rolls Royce shares were down two pence at 257 after earlier rising as high as 264, their highest for more than two months.
Analysts said removal of the limit on foreign share ownership could be modestly positive for BAe and Rolls shares but hopes for a burst of overseas buying should not be overstated.

Zafar Khan, analyst at SocGen, said the removal would be useful for simple policing reasons, since it would avoid messy calculations of overseas share ownership when an international group bought either share.

He said it could also ease the way to any international alliances that the two might be planning, since overseas governments would be more likely to approve an international tie-up if the British market was open.
Yet the short-term impact could be relatively modest, Khan said.
"I think it would be incorrect to say that there is a huge number of guys waiting out there with their chequebooks open waiting to buy these shares," he said.
In addition, a fully-fledged takeover bid for either company remained unlikely, Khan said, with the British government still likely to block a bid even if the 29.5 percent rule no longer applied.
